lines.text: A farmer and a bakery made a deal hundreds of years ago, and it became one of the biggest markets on Earth. Futures.
The farmer worries wheat will be cheap at harvest. The bakery worries it'll be expensive. So today, they agree on a price for later.
That's a futures contract: an agreement to buy or sell a set amount, at a set price, on a set future date.
Unlike an option, it's not a choice. Both sides must follow through, or close the contract before the date.
Today these contracts trade on exchanges. Oil, gold, wheat, even the whole stock market index.
And most traders never want a truck of wheat. They buy the contract, and sell it back before it expires, just for the price move.
You don't pay the full value. You put down a deposit called margin, often just a few percent. That's leverage.
Every single day, the exchange settles up. If the price moved your way, money lands in your account. If not, it's taken out.
Drop below the minimum, and you get a margin call: add money, or your position gets closed.
Why trade futures? Big exposure for little money, markets open nearly all day, and you can bet up or down.
Not financial advice. Leverage cuts both ways, so know how much one tick costs you.
